title: Test doubles: mocks, stubs and fakes
description: Understand the different types of test doubles in React testing, when to use each one, and how to avoid the most common mocking mistakes.

data.text: Test doubles are stand-in objects that replace real collaborators in a test. The term comes from the movie stunt industry: a double does the job of the real actor for a specific scene. In testing, using the right double for the right job keeps tests fast and focused while still giving you useful feedback.

The four most common types are dummies, stubs, spies, mocks, and fakes. Each serves a different purpose, and mixing them up — especially using a mock where a stub would do — is one of the most common sources of brittle test suites.

items: Dummy: Passed around but never used. Fills a parameter list so the test compiles.
Stub: Provides canned answers to calls made during the test. Does not record or fail on unexpected calls.
Spy: Records how it was called — arguments, call count, order — without changing behavior.
Mock: Pre-programmed with expectations. It fails the test if a call was not made or was made with wrong arguments.
Fake: A working implementation with shortcuts, like an in-memory database instead of a real one.

data.text: A stub is the most commonly needed double. It simply returns a value so the component under test can keep running. Here is a stub that provides a fixed user object to a profile widget:

data.text: The stub here only controls the return value. It does not care how many times the hook was called or with what arguments.
A mock asserts behavior. Vitest mocks also spy by default, so you can inspect them after the test. Here is a test that uses both capabilities on an API call:

data.text: A fake is a lightweight but real implementation. In-memory databases, fake timers, or a fake auth service are all fakes. They are heavier than stubs but more trustworthy than mocks because they execute real logic.

data.caption: Using MSW as a fake network layer for integration-style tests

data.title: The mock-everything trap
data.text: Mocking every child component turns your tests into a tautology: you assert that the parent renders the mocks you wrote. The moment a real child changes its API, your test still passes because the mock never changed. Prefer stubs and real components over mocks whenever the real implementation is cheap to run.

data.title: Quick reference
items: Use a dummy to satisfy a parameter list the component does not use.
Use a stub when you need a predictable return value and nothing else.
Use a spy when you need to verify a call happened after the fact.
Use a mock when the contract itself (call count, arguments, order) is what you are testing.
Use a fake when you want real logic without external side effects, such as MSW or an in-memory store.
